<reason>A wins by distinguishing comparable integration from comparable public benefit. B establishes genuine family-life interests, but does not justify its family-first presumption against competing residents’ healthcare needs. A directly answers the pressure questions, identifies dependency and serious separation harm as principled grounds for protection, and distinguishes those protections from general family precedence. B repeatedly relies on superior rootedness despite the comparable-integration condition, while asserting rather than establishing that alternative recruitment tools eliminate economic admissions’ opportunity costs.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A decisively answers B’s contrast between a family’s shared life and an economic applicant’s destination preference: the displaced benefit also belongs to residents needing healthcare. Its accompanying distinction between expected nursing capacity and guaranteed lifelong placement defeats B’s mobility objection without requiring employer-controlled migration.</best_rebuttal>
